title: Six Indian Films Head to Busan International Film Festival 2026
excerpt: From Rima Das's Not a Hero to Anuparna Roy's Venice-bound Lovers in the Blue Night, six Indian features screen at Asia's largest film festival from October 6 — with more titles in the Vision Asia and Wide Angle sections.
body:
• Six Indian films will screen at the 31st Busan International Film Festival, held October 6–15 at the Busan Cinema Center in South Korea, in the festival's 'A Window on Asian Cinema' section.
  • Assamese filmmaker Rima Das returns to Busan with the coming-of-age drama Not a Hero, after her Village Rockstars 2 won the Kim Jiseok Award at the festival.
  • Anuparna Roy — the first Indian filmmaker to win Best Director at Venice — brings Lovers in the Blue Night, which also screens at Venice; Roy will additionally serve on Busan's shorts jury.
  • Indian cinema also extends to other sections: Selvi and Birds in the Dark in Vision Asia, and Salt Electric in the Wide Angle short-film competition.

Six Indian films have been selected for the 31st Busan International Film Festival, which runs October 6 to 15 at the Busan Cinema Center in South Korea — a lineup that puts Indian independent cinema firmly at the centre of Asia's largest film festival. The six will screen in 'A Window on Asian Cinema', the festival's prominent non-competitive section showcasing new and notable works by filmmakers from across Asia, according to Press Trust of India.

The Lineup

The headline names are Rima Das and Anuparna Roy. Das, the Assamese filmmaker known for Village Rockstars, Bulbul Can Sing and Tora's Husband, returns to Busan with Not a Hero, a coming-of-age drama about an 11-year-old boy sent from the city to live in a village. Her association with the festival runs deep: Village Rockstars 2 premiered at Busan and won the Kim Jiseok Award.

"I have a long association with the Busan International Film Festival, and I've always valued the space it creates for Asian cinema, a place where stories rooted in very different cultures and realities can find a wider conversation."

— Rima Das, filmmaker

Roy — who became the first Indian filmmaker to win the Best Director award at the Venice Film Festival for her debut feature Songs of Forgotten Trees — brings Lovers in the Blue Night, which has also been selected for Venice. Roy will also serve as a shorts jury member at Busan. "The film is also going to Busan, and that journey will probably feel more like our first Venice experience," Roy told Homegrown India. "I'm also going to Busan as a juror, which is a huge responsibility."

The other four titles in the section: Leo Thaddeus' Malayalam feature Chevittorma (The Soul Whisperer), starring Dileesh Pothan and Pauly Valsan; Vishwendra Singh's Khoriya, a Nepali-Hindi drama about two half-brothers running a poultry farm on Delhi's outskirts when a bird flu outbreak threatens their livelihood; Sahil Shah's Birds on Ice; and Sandeep Kumar Paul's About an Intimate Matter. Three of the six — The Soul Whisperer, Khoriya and Birds on Ice — will have their world premieres in the section, according to Homegrown India.

Context & Background

BIFF has become a launchpad for Indian indie cinema. The 'A Window on Asian Cinema' section has a track record of surfacing films that later travel the festival circuit and find global streaming homes. Roy's arc is the clearest proof of momentum: from her Venice Orizzonti debut to an Asian premiere at Busan within a single season.

The Indian presence extends beyond the six. Sailesh Rathnakumar's Selvi — the debut feature of the Prague Film School alumnus — heads to Busan for its world premiere, selected alongside Shashank Walia's Birds in the Dark in the Vision Asia section, while Paromita Dhar's Salt Electric will compete in the Wide Angle: Asian Short Film Competition, according to e2mag.

Impact & Analysis

What stands out is the regional spread. Assamese, Malayalam, Nepali-Hindi and Hindi-language work sits alongside each other — this is not a Bollywood contingent but a portrait of India's independent film economy, where festivals remain the primary route to audiences and distributors. Alongside the screenings, Platform Busan (October 10–13) brings five Indian filmmakers — including Garima Pura, co-writer of the Oscar-winning The Elephant Whisperers — to pitch new projects to international financiers, according to Devdiscourse.

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, festival selections are the early signal for what lands on streaming platforms months later — Not a Hero and Lovers in the Blue Night are likely future festival-to-platform titles. South Korea itself hosts a large South Asian expatriate community, and BIFF screenings with English subtitles have become gathering points for Indian cinema lovers in Busan and Seoul.

What's Next

The festival opens October 6. Watch for the Asian premieres of Roy's film — fresh off Venice — and the three world premieres in the Indian sextet. Distribution deals announced during Busan's Asian Contents & Film Market will determine when diaspora audiences outside Korea can see these films.
